title: Earth as a Planet
tagline: The shape and size of the Earth, its place in the solar system and the conditions that make life possible

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). All measurements quoted are standard astronomical and geodetic values. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Describe the shape and size of the Earth and explain why the equatorial diameter is longer than the polar diameter.
State the position of the Earth in the solar system and distinguish rotation from revolution.
Explain the causes of day and night, of the seasons and of the five major circles of latitude.
Identify the conditions on the Earth that support life.

overview.intro: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only planet known to carry life. Its shape is not a perfect sphere but a slightly flattened sphere called an oblate spheroid, which is why the equatorial diameter of about 12,756 km is about 44 km longer than the polar diameter of about 12,712 km. The Earth is tilted by 23.5 degrees to the plane of its orbit, and that single fact explains the seasons, the length of day and night, and the existence of the polar day and polar night. Beneath the thin skin of atmosphere lies a surface that is about 71 per cent water and 29 per cent land, and it is the combination of liquid water, a protective atmosphere, a magnetic field and a workable range of temperature that makes life possible.

facts.label: Position in the solar system
facts.value: Third planet from the Sun, between Venus and Mars

facts.label: Mean radius
facts.value: About 6,371 km; equatorial radius 6,378 km, polar radius 6,357 km

facts.label: Axis of rotation
facts.value: Tilted 23.5 degrees to the plane of the orbit of the Earth

facts.label: Surface covered by water
facts.value: About 71 per cent; the remaining 29 per cent is land

learn.title: The shape and size of the Earth

blocks.text: To an observer standing on the surface the Earth looks flat, because the radius of the Earth is very large compared with the small part of it that any one person can see. The evidence that it is a sphere comes from several independent observations. A ship that is far out at sea is seen hull first and its masts last, which shows that the surface curves away from the observer. The shadow of the Earth on the Moon during a lunar eclipse is always round. The horizon of the Earth seen from a high altitude at sunset is circular. And the fact that different parts of the Earth experience different local times shows that the Sun cannot shine on all of it at once.

items.meaning: The shape of a perfectly round body, with every point on the surface equally distant from the centre.
A sphere flattened at the poles and bulged at the equator; the true shape of the Earth.
The irregular surface of the Earth as it would be if sea level were extended under the continents; the surface used in mapping.
The average value of the equatorial and polar radii, about 6,371 km, used as the Earth's radius in calculations.

items: The equatorial diameter is about 12,756 km and the polar diameter about 12,712 km, so the Earth is flattened by about 44 km across.
The average radius of the Earth is about 6,371 km and its surface area about 510 million square kilometres.
The circumference at the Equator is about 40,075 km and the distance through the poles about 40,008 km.
About 71 per cent of the surface is covered by water and about 29 per cent by land, so nearly three-quarters of the Earth is ocean.
The irregularities of the geoid are small: the highest mountain, Mount Everest, is only about 0.14 per cent of the Earth's radius.

items.text: Express the Earth's average radius in kilometres in terms of its diameter.
items.note: The diameter is about 12,742 km, so the radius is half of it, about 6,371 km. Any question that gives a diameter and asks for a radius needs this halving first.

items.text: If the Earth's circumference at the Equator is 40,075 km, what is the approximate radius in kilometres?
items.note: Radius = circumference divided by 2 pi = 40,075 / (2 x 3.1416) = 40,075 / 6.2832 = about 6,378 km, which agrees with the measured equatorial radius.

learn.title: The Earth in the solar system: rotation and revolution

blocks.text: The Earth revolves round the Sun once in about 365.25 days, and this revolution plus the 23.5 degree axial tilt produces the year and the seasons. The Earth also rotates on its own axis once in about 24 hours, and this rotation produces day and night. The direction of revolution is anticlockwise when the solar system is viewed from above the North Pole, and the same is true of the Earth's rotation, which is why the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.

blocks.caption: Table: rotation compared with revolution
rows: Spinning of the Earth on its own axis
Movement of the Earth round the Sun
An oval path called the orbit
The year and, with the tilt, the seasons

items: The orbit of the Earth is an ellipse, and the Sun sits at one focus of that ellipse.
The Earth is closest to the Sun around 4 January, when it is at perihelion, and farthest around 4 July, at aphelion.
The 23.5 degree tilt stays pointed in the same direction in space all through the year, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for half of it and away for the other half.
The circle of latitude that is tilted towards the Sun receives direct rays and has its longest day at the June solstice.
The poles receive oblique or no rays for part of the year, producing the polar day and polar night.

items.text: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has its summer in June while the Southern Hemisphere has its winter.
items.note: From March to September the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun, so the Northern Hemisphere receives more direct sunlight over a longer daylight period and its temperatures rise. At the same time the South Pole is tilted away from the Sun, so the Southern Hemisphere receives oblique rays over shorter days and its temperatures fall. The two seasons are therefore always opposite.

items.text: Why is an ordinary year 365 days long, and how is the leap year used?
items.note: The Earth takes 365 and a quarter days to complete one revolution round the Sun, and that is the length of a year. The quarter day has to be dealt with, because the calendar works in whole days and the leftover would otherwise push the dates slowly out of step with the seasons. The year is therefore made a leap year of 366 days every fourth year, so that the extra day is collected and added to the calendar. The true year is in fact a little shorter than 365 and a quarter days, and that is why a century year is not a leap year unless it is divisible by 400.

learn.title: The five circles of latitude and the heat zones

blocks.text: The five important circles of latitude are the Arctic Circle at 66.5 degrees north, the Tropic of Cancer at 23.5 degrees north, the Equator at 0 degrees, the Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5 degrees south and the Antarctic Circle at 66.5 degrees south. They mark out the hot, temperate and cold zones, because the angle at which the Sun's rays strike the Earth changes from the Equator towards the poles.

blocks.caption: Table: the heat zones
rows: Between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
Direct, twice a year at the solstices
Between the tropics and the polar circles
Moderate warmth in summer and coolness in winter
North of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle
Extremely cold, with polar day and polar night

items: The Tropics are the northernmost and southernmost points at which the Sun can be directly overhead, that is 23.5 degrees north and south of the Equator.
Within the Arctic and Antarctic Circles the Sun does not rise at all on some days in winter and does not set at all on some days in summer.
The heat zones are bounded by the tropics and the polar circles and are the reason the Earth's surface has climatic belts rather than one single climate.
The Equator is the longest line of latitude at about 40,075 km and divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
The Equator passes through the middle of the great land masses of South America and Africa and through Indonesia.

blocks.text: Life as we know it needs a narrow set of conditions, and the Earth happens to provide all of them at once. The first requirement is a suitable range of temperature, which liquid water and the chemistry of carbon depend on. The second is liquid water, which is the solvent in which the chemical reactions of life take place. The third is the right atmosphere, with oxygen for respiration and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. The fourth is a magnetic field and a protective ozone layer, which together reduce the harm done by solar and cosmic radiation.

items.meaning: A layer of ozone in the stratosphere that absorbs much of the harmful ultra-violet radiation from the Sun.
The field around the Earth that deflects charged particles of the solar wind and so protects the surface from radiation.
The warming of the lower atmosphere by the absorption of outgoing terrestrial radiation by gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour.
The zone of life on the Earth, extending from the deepest ocean trenches to the lower edge of the atmosphere and a little below the surface of the crust.

items: Liquid water exists as a liquid, a solid and a gas over the range of temperatures found on the Earth's surface.
Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 per cent of the dry atmosphere by volume.
The atmosphere also screens the Earth from meteoroids, most of which burn up before reaching the ground.
The tilt of 23.5 degrees never varies enough to change the seasons of a whole hemisphere at once, which keeps the annual temperature range moderate.
The Moon's pull keeps the ocean tides working, and the resulting coastal erosion and sedimentation are part of the constant recycling of the land surface.

figures.caption: Figure: The Earth as an oblate spheroid
figures.description: The Earth is flattened at the poles and bulged at the Equator because the centrifugal effect of rotation is greatest at the Equator. The equatorial radius is about 6,378 km and the polar radius about 6,357 km.

figures.caption: Figure: Rotation, revolution and the 23.5 degree tilt
figures.description: The Earth spins on a tilted axis once a day and travels round the Sun once a year. Because the axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space, each hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun for half of the year, which produces the seasons.
labels: direct rays at the Tropic of Cancer

keyPoints: The Earth is an oblate spheroid, flattened at the poles and bulged at the Equator.
Equatorial radius 6,378 km, polar radius 6,357 km, mean radius about 6,371 km.
About 71 per cent of the surface is covered by water and 29 per cent by land.
The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and revolves round it once in 365.25 days.
Rotation on the tilted axis takes about 24 hours and produces day and night.
The axis is tilted 23.5 degrees, and this tilt is the cause of the seasons.
The five circles of latitude are the Arctic Circle, Tropic of Cancer, Equator, Tropic of Capricorn and Antarctic Circle.
Between the tropics the Sun's rays are direct; towards the poles they become oblique.
Life needs liquid water, a moderate temperature range, an atmosphere with oxygen and carbon dioxide, and protection from radiation.
The geoid is the real, irregular shape of the Earth, used as the datum for mapping.
examFocus: Questions often ask for the shape of the Earth together with one reason for the bulge at the Equator; the effect of the centrifugal force during rotation is the expected answer.
When comparing rotation with revolution, tabulate the time taken, the axis or path, and the result produced; that is the format most questions use.
For seasons questions, remember that the cause is the constant tilt of the axis and not the changing distance from the Sun.
Naming the five circles of latitude in the correct order from north to south, with the correct latitudes, is a standard one-mark recall question.
A good answer on conditions for life always names water, temperature, atmosphere and radiation protection, and gives a reason for each.

vocabulary.meaning: A sphere flattened at the poles and bulged at the Equator, which is the true shape of the Earth.
The irregular surface of the Earth with sea level continued under the continents, used as the reference surface for maps.
The spinning of the Earth on its own axis once in about 24 hours, which causes day and night.
The movement of the Earth round the Sun once in about 365.25 days, which causes the year.
The point of the Earth's orbit nearest the Sun, reached around 4 January.
The point of the Earth's orbit farthest from the Sun, reached around 4 July.
The day on which the Sun is directly overhead at a tropic, marking the longest and shortest days of the year.
The zone of the Earth in which living organisms exist.

questions.prompt: The true shape of the Earth is best described as:
questions.explanation: The Earth is a sphere flattened at the poles and bulged at the Equator because the centrifugal effect of rotation is strongest at the Equator. Its polar radius is about 6,357 km against an equatorial radius of about 6,378 km.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'a perfect sphere', which ignores the measurable flattening of about 44 km across.

questions.prompt: The equatorial radius of the Earth is approximately:
questions.explanation: The equatorial radius is about 6,378 km and the polar radius about 6,357 km. The value 6,371 km is the mean radius, which is the average of the two.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 6,371 km, which is the mean radius and not the equatorial radius asked for.

questions.prompt: The Earth revolves round the Sun once in approximately:
questions.explanation: One revolution of the Earth round the Sun takes about 365.25 days, which is one year. The 24 hours is the time taken by one rotation, that is one day.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing revolution with rotation and giving 24 hours.

questions.prompt: The seasons are caused mainly by:
options: The constant 23.5 degree tilt of the Earth's axis
The changing distance of the Earth from the Sun
The changing length of the day at the Equator
questions.answer: The constant 23.5 degree tilt of the Earth's axis
questions.explanation: The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for half the year and away from it for the other half. The change in distance between perihelion and aphelion is far too small to produce the seasons.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the changing distance from the Sun, which contributes almost nothing to the difference between summer and winter.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the axis of the Earth is tilted at an angle of ________ to the plane of its orbit.
questions.explanation: The Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees to the plane of its orbit, and this constant tilt is the reason for the seasons and for the existence of the heat zones.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 66.5 degrees, which is the latitude of the polar circles rather than the tilt of the axis.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the time taken by the Earth to complete one rotation on its axis, which is one day, is about ________ hours.
questions.explanation: One rotation of the Earth on its axis takes about 24 hours and produces the alternation of day and night.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 365.25, which is the time for one revolution round the Sun.

questions.prompt: Give two pieces of evidence that the Earth is a sphere.
questions.answer: First, the shadow of the Earth on the Moon during a lunar eclipse is always round. Second, a ship far out at sea is seen hull first and its masts last, because the surface curves away below the line of sight. Other acceptable evidence is the circular horizon seen from a high altitude and the fact that different longitudes have different local times.
questions.explanation: Each observation can only be explained by a curved surface, so two independent observations together make the case for a spherical Earth.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one piece of evidence, which earns fewer marks than the two that the question asks for.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer in June while the Southern Hemisphere has winter in the same months.
questions.answer: The Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees and keeps pointing in the same direction in space. From March to September the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun, so the Northern Hemisphere receives more direct sunlight for longer days and its temperature rises. At the same time the South Pole is tilted away from the Sun, so the Southern Hemisphere receives more oblique sunlight over shorter days and its temperature falls.
questions.explanation: Because the tilt is constant and opposite for the two hemispheres, their seasons are always six months apart.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the Northern Hemisphere is nearer the Sun in June, which is false and confuses the cause of the seasons.

questions.prompt: Name the five circles of latitude in order from north to south and give the latitude of each.
questions.answer: The Arctic Circle at 66.5 degrees north; the Tropic of Cancer at 23.5 degrees north; the Equator at 0 degrees; the Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5 degrees south; and the Antarctic Circle at 66.5 degrees south.
questions.explanation: The two polar circles and the two tropics sit symmetrically about the Equator, and together with the Equator they divide the Earth into the heat zones.
questions.commonMistake: Putting the Equator in the middle and reversing the order of the circles, or giving 23.5 degrees for the polar circles.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between rotation and revolution of the Earth, giving the time taken and the result produced by each, and state one effect of each on daily life.
questions.answer: Rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its own axis once in about 24 hours; it produces the alternation of day and night and the daily apparent movement of the Sun across the sky. Revolution is the movement of the Earth round the Sun along its elliptical orbit once in about 365.25 days; it produces the year and, together with the 23.5 degree tilt, the seasons. An effect of rotation is that a place on the Equator experiences sunrise roughly every 24 hours while a place near the poles experiences long summer days and long winter nights. An effect of revolution is that a school year and the harvest calendar fall at the same season each year and that crops in the two hemispheres ripen at opposite times of the year.
questions.explanation: The two motions differ in axis, path, duration and result, and a full answer separates all four before giving the daily-life example.
questions.commonMistake: Describing both motions as a single daily and yearly movement without naming the axis and the path for each.

questions.prompt: Explain why the conditions for life exist on the Earth but not on the planet nearest to it, Venus.
questions.answer: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and lies about 42 million kilometres closer to it than the Earth. That small difference in distance is enough to change the whole situation, because the nearer a planet is to the Sun, the more intense is the solar heating. Venus has a very dense atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide, which traps the incoming heat so effectively that its surface temperature is about 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Its surface pressure is about 90 times that of the Earth, which crushes any land vehicle, and the clouds of sulphuric acid rule out liquid water on the surface. The Earth, at 149.6 million kilometres from the Sun, receives the right intensity of radiation for liquid water to exist over most of its surface, holds an atmosphere with free oxygen and carbon dioxide, and has an ozone layer and a magnetic field that screen harmful radiation. The Earth also has a stable orbit that has allowed the conditions to persist for billions of years.
questions.explanation: The distance from the Sun sets the temperature, which controls whether water can be liquid, and that in turn decides whether an atmosphere like ours and life itself can exist.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that Venus is too hot, without explaining the chain from distance to temperature to the state of water to the atmosphere.
